extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in philosophy of science, history of science, and specialists interested in the emergence of scientific disciplines (especially paleontology)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the conditions and mechanisms by which new scientific specializations (disciplines) emerge, using an evolutionary/Darwinian model and historical case (evolutionary paleontology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Branching most likely when there are no intermediate phenotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Branching events are most likely to occur when there are no intermediate phenotypes (illustrated by the 'toast vs. grape' example: toast-eating ability is something one either has or doesn’t have).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trait/ability is effectively binary, two selection regimes can emerge (one pushing variants toward the toast-eating optimum and the other toward the grape-eating optimum). In contrast, if all members can perform both tasks (continuous/overlapping phenotypes), a single selective process will drive the population to a single optimum. Example/anti-pattern: the extreme toast vs. grape case shows clear branching potential; when abilities overlap, branching is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness of problem-solving methods in practice space
rubrics_metrics.description: If the methods of solving the new problem are close enough in practice space to reach via a sufficiently plastic application of existing methods, there won’t be the disruptive pressure required to split the community into distinct specializations; if qualitatively distinct problem-solving methods are required, an autonomous new specialization may emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how 'far' the new problem is in practice/method space from existing methods. If existing practitioners can adapt their toolkit with small variations, no new specialization is likely. If qualitatively different methods (not mere variations) are required, practitioners will diverge. Example: two statisticians with identical training may still branch into data science vs. biostatistics if their problem domains are distinct enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability of specialization varies inversely with marginal utility of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability that a new specialization will emerge varies inversely with the marginal utility of progress in an established specialization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As it becomes harder to make important gains within a parent discipline (marginal utility of further progress declines), relative opportunities in a new domain increase, raising the chance of branching. Holton's graph and Holton/Mulkay examples: branching tends to occur where the slope of 'undiscovered interesting ideas' levels off—the point where making major progress in the parent field becomes less probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major contributions to parent specialization largely made
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the major contributions to a given specialization have been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of three core conditions that favor emergence of a new specialization: when a field's 'low-hanging fruit' is exhausted and major novel contributions are scarce, practitioners have stronger incentives to migrate to or create new specializations. This is listed explicitly as condition (1) in the text's summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: A new problem of widely appreciated significance
rubrics_metrics.description: A new problem has been identified whose significance is widely appreciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed explicitly as condition (2). For a new specialization to endure, the problem's significance must be recognizable not only to those who can investigate it but also to a broad range of specialists (so resources/support can be garnered). Anti-pattern: a problem that is important only to a tiny subgroup and not recognized by the broader community is less likely to found a new discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigating the new problem requires specific investigative tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigating the new problem requires a specific set of investigative tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed explicitly as condition (3). If addressing the problem demands unique tools or recondite techniques that most practitioners cannot easily master, a new specialization can form around the mastery and use of those tools. Mulkay's point: instruments whose competent operation is recondite can spur entire specializations to grow around that technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence depends on recognition by practitioners outside the discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of a new discipline's existence depends on recognition of practitioners outside the discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner must convince a broad range of specialists that the research is worthwhile to obtain resources/support. The text stresses that one cannot simply announce a new discipline—external recognition is necessary for real autonomy and persistence. This connects to the need for significance to be widely appreciated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control/monopolization of some defensible resource
rubrics_metrics.description: The development of a discipline requires 'control of some defensible resource'—identifying a set of scientific problems that practitioners of the new discipline alone are equipped to 'metabolize.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopolizing a defensible resource increases the degree to which the discipline's practices contribute to goals that matter more to its practitioners than to outsiders, aiding isolation and enabling selection among practices (intrinsicality condition). This is instrumental for a group of practices to function as a Darwinian population subject to evolutionary change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of overlap/common ground between practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: The less common ground there is between practitioners who engage in one practice and practitioners who engage in the other practice, the more probable it is that the single community will fissure into two specializations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess overlap in subject matter, methods, vocabulary, and resource/territory. High overlap reduces disruptive pressure and keeps a single community intact; low overlap increases chances of branching. This captures the 'isolation' spatial/ecological analogy used in the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of exclusive methodological training/choice
rubrics_metrics.description: When each practitioner will have to choose to acquire one set of methods or another (i.e., exclusive or incompatible training paths), an autonomous specialization is more likely to emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If competent operation of certain methods or technologies is impracticable to combine with mastery of other subject-matter demands, practitioners polarize around distinct skill-sets, facilitating specialization (example: recondite technologies leading to separate specializations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers to communication depend on scale/dimension of lexical divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Incommensurability does not automatically imply ineffective communication; barriers depend on the scale and the dimension of lexical divergence, not on mere untranslatability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a branching event entails untranslatable or ineffective communication, consider how extensive lexical/semantic divergence is. Large-scale divergence may prevent easy translation without 'going native,' but lesser divergence may still permit effective (if imperfect) communication. This nuance cautions against using communication failure as sole evidence for incommensurability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogy and training orientation toward disciplinary autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: For a field to achieve autonomy, training and scholarship must be geared toward the discipline's distinctive theoretical and methodological aims (e.g., paleontology training should emphasize biology/evolutionary theory rather than purely stratigraphy/geology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate curricula and training: supplying students with the theoretical and methodological tools required to detect the discipline's unique phenomena is essential for autonomy. Anti-pattern: training that leaves practitioners primarily as handmaidens to neighboring disciplines undermines independent disciplinary identity and capacity to claim unique contributions.
